extracted.intended_audience: NSF program officers, external reviewers, and researchers applying for NSF research funding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating NSF research proposals using the two National Science Board-approved merit review criteria (Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts), including the five elements considered for both criteria and examples of broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential for the proposed project to advance knowledge and understanding within its own field or across different fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the two main NSF merit review criteria and should be evaluated in light of the five elements considered for both criteria (potential for transformative concepts; strategic plan quality; qualifications; resources; importance/value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential for the proposed project to benefit society and contribute to the achievement of specific, desired societal outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Evaluate how the project will benefit society and lead to desired outcomes. Examples of broader impacts (non-exhaustive):
- Increased participation of women, persons with disabilities, and underrepresented minorities in STEM
- Improved STEM education and educator development at any level
- Increased public scientific literacy and engagement with science and technology
- Improved well-being of individuals in society
- Development of a globally competitive STEM workforce
- Increased partnerships between academia, industry, and others
- Improved national security
- Increased economic competitiveness of the US
- Enhanced infrastructure for research and education
Also assess Broader Impacts using the five elements considered for both criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for transformative concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: To what extent do the proposed activities suggest and explore creative, original or potentially transformative concepts?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of five elements reviewers should consider when applying both Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts. Look for novelty, creativity, and potential to change paradigms or open new research directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic plan quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the plan for carrying out the proposed activities well-reasoned, well-organized and based on a sound rationale? Does the plan incorporate a mechanism to assess success?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity, organization, rationale, feasibility, and presence of evaluation/assessment measures. This element applies to both Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: How well qualified is the individual, team, or institution to conduct the proposed activities?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the PI(s)'s and team's expertise, track record, and institutional support relative to project needs; applies to evaluation of both criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there adequate resources available to the PI (either at the home institution or through collaborations) to carry out the proposed activities?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate availability of facilities, equipment, collaborators, and other resources that affect feasibility and likelihood of success for both Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance/value
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the PI(s) made the case for the proposed activities, both in terms of advancing knowledge and benefitting society?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the overall significance and value proposition of the project—its contribution to advancing knowledge (Intellectual Merit) and to societal outcomes (Broader Impacts). This is one of the five cross-cutting elements for both criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review process and reviewer selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical procedures by which NSF program officers obtain external evaluations of proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSF program officers typically identify external reviewers who are experts in the fields represented by the proposal. Reviews may be conducted by ad hoc reviewers, a panel of experts, or a combination of both. Consider that different review formats (panel vs. ad hoc) may affect how criteria are applied and discussed.
